transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-05
Start: 15:00 PST
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Lee (Redwood AE), Priya Menon (Redwood SE), Samira Ortiz (CTO - Oceanic Retail), Liam Nguyen (Lead Engineer), Arjun Patel (Security), Maya Ruiz (Product)

Summary (auto): Quick SDK integration walkthrough focused on Python/TypeScript quickstarts, auth and env setup, and next steps for a short pilot. Security questions raised around SSO/KMS and private deployments.

Topics: SDK quickstart, API auth (API key vs SAML), env vars and secrets, sample code (Python/TS), Console demo for keys and billing, Redwood Optimize suggestions for batching/quantization, pilot/benchmarks.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan: hey everyone thanks for joining, can you hear me ok?
[00:03] Samira: yep loud and clear, thanks Jordan.
[00:05] Priya: hi all, i'll be running through the SDK quickstarts and the console bits, jordan will cover pricing/next steps.
[00:12] Liam: quick note we have a couple infra folks on standby in case we get deep into network stuff.
[00:17] Jordan: perfect, thanks. quick check, you wanted python and typescript examples right?
[00:21] Samira: correct, and also we need to understand auth and how SSO would work for our developers.
[00:26] Priya: great, i'll start with the python quickstart. the repo is small, main flow is pip install redwood-client, set REDWOOD_API_KEY in your env, then call client.generate - it's intentionally light.
[00:40] Priya: code snippet: from redwood import RedwoodClient; client = RedwoodClient(api_key=os.getenv('REDWOOD_API_KEY')) ; resp = client.generate(prompt) - typical.
[00:52] Liam: are there official SDKs for both python and typescript?
[00:56] Priya: yes, both. TS is an npm package, very similar: import Redwood from '@redwood/inference'; const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_API_KEY });
[01:06] Maya: what's the recommended auth pattern for server-side apps vs client-side?
[01:10] Priya: server-side use API keys stored in your secret manager; client-side you should proxy through your backend to avoid exposing keys. we also support SSO/SAML for user access to the console and role-based API key management for teams.
[01:21] Arjun: and for enterprise, can we integrate with our okta and KMS?
[01:25] Jordan: yes, we do SAML/SSO with Okta and others, and for Private deployments we integrate with customer KMS/HSM for key wrapping. i'll send the integration doc.
[01:36] Priya: demo time - i'll share my screen, opening the Console. (screen share noise)
[01:42] Priya: Console view: projects -> keys, you can create scoped API keys, set permissions (read/generate/embed), and rotate keys. also see usage dashboards per model.
[01:56] Liam: can keys be limited to a route or model?
[01:59] Priya: yes, route-level and model-level scoping. you can also set rate limits on keys.
[02:06] Priya: now back to code; quick note on environment files: we usually set REDWOOD_API_KEY, REDWOOD_ENV (prod/staging), and REDWOOD_REGION for routing. sample .env in quickstart repo.
[02:19] Samira: does the client support streaming? we have UIs that benefit from token streaming.
[02:23] Priya: streaming is supported in both SDKs; in python we have client.stream_generate with an iterator, in TS you can subscribe to events. caveat: streaming behavior can change with model and region, but it's stable on hosted offering.
[02:38] Priya: now a quick demo of the optimize suggestions - Optimize flags some routes for batching and suggests a quantized variant if latency tolerances permit.
[02:47] Jordan: just to interject, Optimize is where you get cost/perf tradeoffs - it will recommend batching sizes and whether to use a quantized variant or bigger model for quality.
[02:58] Maya: that sounds useful. what about caching? prefix caching?
[03:02] Priya: yes, we have prefix/KV cache features; for chat apps the KV cache cuts token costs for repeated context.
[03:10] Liam: network layout question: we run in GCP, will there be egress or VPC peering for private?
[03:16] Jordan: for Redwood Private we support VPC peering and private link options - no public egress required. for Dedicated you can also get customer-dedicated pools in the same region.
[03:29] Arjun: security - do you store logs and how long? encryption at rest?
[03:33] Jordan: hosted logs can be configured; by default we keep short-term logs for debugging, but enterprise customers can opt-out and send logs to their SIEM. we support encryption at rest and customer managed keys for Private. SOC2 docs are available.
[03:48] Samira: can you walk through an example env for a staging server and CI?
[03:51] Priya: sure - staging CI example: set REDWOOD_API_KEY as a secret in your CI provider, use REDWOOD_ENV=staging, lock key permissions so it can only call generate endpoints, and run smoke tests that validate outputs. we include a sample github action in the repo.
[04:07] Liam: any gotchas with rate limiting and retry logic in the SDKs?
[04:11] Priya: SDKs include basic exponential backoff by default; we recommend additional client-side batching for high qps and use dedicated pools if you need SLOs.
[04:20] Samira: we have privacy constraints, some data can't leave our VPC. how does that work with hosted?
[04:24] Jordan: hosted won't fit that use case - for those you want Private deployment or Dedicated with private networking. we'll map cost differences in the follow-up.
[04:33] Priya: switching to TypeScript code sample - here's an example that does streaming and handles partials: (reads sample) there's a small diff in event handling but otherwise same flow.
[04:44] Liam: can we run local dev with a mock server?
[04:47] Priya: yes repo includes a mock server script; set REDWOOD_MOCK=true to avoid hitting prod. good for offline dev and unit tests.
[04:55] Arjun: audit logs - are they tamper-evident? retention policy?
[04:59] Jordan: audit logs are part of the enterprise package, they're pushed to customer SIEM or can be exported; we support append-only logs and can provide accounting for compliance.
[05:10] Maya: any recommended prompts or prompt templates in quickstarts?
[05:13] Priya: we include a few templates for instruction tuning prompts and structured output examples - also a small eval harness to test quality regressions.
[05:24] Samira: let's talk pilot scope - we want a quick POC to validate latency for our checkout flow and compare cost across batching configs.
[05:30] Jordan: sounds good - typical pilot is 1-2 weeks, we run a focused benchmark with your sample workload and share a spreadsheet with latency and token cost breakdown.
[05:40] Priya: to run the benchmark we'll need sample traffic profile: qps, average sequence length, the concurrency you expect, examples of prompts.
[05:47] Liam: i'll put together a sample trace and share.
[05:50] Arjun: we'll need the security questionnaire before pilot starts.
[05:53] Jordan: yes we'll share SOC2 and the security pack, and Priya will include the SAML metadata example.
[06:00] Priya: quick gotcha: when using client-side streaming in TS, ensure you're on the latest npm release - older versions had a slightly different handshake.
[06:10] Samira: ok good to know.
[06:12] Priya: final demo bit - show quickstart repo dir: /quickstarts/python, /quickstarts/typescript, sample .env.example, mock-server, github actions.
[06:25] Jordan: recapping next steps: we send pricing, quickstarts, security docs, schedule pilot, and collect profiles from Liam. any other blockers?
[06:35] Samira: no blockers, we'll review and get dates. thanks both.
[06:38] Jordan: thanks everyone.

(Transcript ends - occasional transcription errors: "K-V cache" vs KV cache, some proper nouns mis-recognized.)
